children.title: Preconditioned Inner Solves
children.top_down_role: Inner-system preconditioning coordinated with the outer splitting metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioned Inner Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditions inner systems while measuring accuracy in a metric compatible with the outer splitting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inner system \(H_ku=b_k\), choose an invertible preconditioner \(P_k\) and apply a compatible iterative solver to \(P_k^{-1}H_ku=P_k^{-1}b_k\). Compute residuals \(r^j=b_k-H_ku^j\) and stop only when a declared norm compatible with the outer splitting metric satisfies \(\lVert r^j\rVert_{W_k^{-1}}\le\varepsilon_k\), where \(W_k\) is positive definite and \(\varepsilon_k\) is the prescribed inner tolerance. Return \(u^j\), the unpreconditioned residual, and its metric norm. Preconditioning changes the computational representation of the solve, not the target equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply an invertible preconditioner, but certify inner accuracy using the original equation and a norm coordinated with the outer splitting metric.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\) is invertible and the preconditioned operator satisfies the requirements of the chosen iterative method.
\(W_k\) is positive definite and matches the outer method's declared residual metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output solves the original inner equation to tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\) in the coordinated metric.

notation.meaning: unpreconditioned residual at inner iteration j

children.title: Warm-Started Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Reuse of previous block solutions or active structures in nested solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Started Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initializes each nested block solve from the preceding outer iterate or reusable active structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), let the block subproblem be \(u_k^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_u\phi_k(u)\). Initialize its inner solver with the preceding accepted block solution \(u_k^0=u_{k-1}\), optionally together with previously validated active-set or working-set state. Run the chosen inner method until its current stopping rule is satisfied, then accept \(u_k\). Discard or repair inherited structural state whenever current feasibility, complementarity, dimension, or model-version checks fail. Warm starting changes only initialization and reusable state; it does not weaken the current subproblem's acceptance criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start each block solve from the prior accepted solution and validated structural state, while retaining the current subproblem's full stopping test.
assumptions_latex: Successive subproblems share compatible variable spaces and representations.
Inherited active or working sets are checked against the current subproblem before use.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted warm-started solution satisfies the same current stopping rule as a cold-started solve.

children.title: Separable Execution Interfaces

children.title: Parallel Proximal Blocks
children.top_down_role: Independent proximal evaluations across separable operator blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Proximal Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous proximal evaluation for separable blocks with a synchronization point before coupled updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}f_i(x_i)\) on the product Hilbert space \(\mathcal H=\mathcal H_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal H_p\). For each \(i\), let \(M_i\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive, and let \(\gamma_i>0\). Given a common snapshot \(v^k=(v_1^k,\ldots,v_p^k)\), evaluate independently and concurrently \[x_i^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{M_i}_{\gamma_i f_i}(v_i^k)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in\mathcal H_i}\left\{f_i(x_i)+\frac{1}{2\gamma_i}\lVert x_i-v_i^k\rVert_{M_i}^2\right\},\quad i=1,\ldots,p.\] Synchronize the completed blocks before any update depending jointly on \((x_1^{k+1},\ldots,x_p^{k+1})\). With \(M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1/\gamma_1,\ldots,M_p/\gamma_p)\), return the assembled vector \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{M}_{f}(v^k)\), where \(\operatorname{prox}^{M}_{f}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal H}\{f(x)+\tfrac12\lVert x-v\rVert_M^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a separable convex objective, compute every strongly positive metric-proximal block concurrently from one common snapshot, synchronize, and assemble the corresponding product-metric proximal point.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathcal H_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
Each \(M_i\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive, and each \(\gamma_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The synchronized assembled vector equals \(\operatorname{prox}^{M}_{f}(v^k)\) for \(M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1/\gamma_1,\ldots,M_p/\gamma_p)\).

notation.meaning: block proximal map in metric M_i with parameter gamma_i
product metric with blocks M_i divided by gamma_i

children.title: Centralized Consensus Interface
children.top_down_role: Worker-local block computations coordinated through a shared consensus component.

knowledge_statements.title: Centralized Consensus Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous consensus ADMM with worker-local proximal updates and one central averaging component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given proper closed convex functions \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), solve \(\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_m,z}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(x_i=z\). Choose \(\rho>0\), initialize \(z^0,u_i^0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and, for \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute in parallel \[x_i^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{f_i/\rho}(z^k-u_i^k),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] The central component then computes \[z^{k+1}=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(x_i^{k+1}+u_i^k),\qquad u_i^{k+1}=u_i^k+x_i^{k+1}-z^{k+1}.\] Stop when prescribed primal and dual residual tests hold; output \(z^{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers evaluate local proximal maps in parallel; a central component averages their shifted iterates, broadcasts consensus, and coordinates dual updates until residual tolerances hold.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex for every \(i\).
\(\rho>0\), and all workers complete each synchronous iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface implements two-block consensus ADMM for the constraints \(x_i=z\).

notation.meaning: Scaled dual variable for worker i's consensus constraint.

children.title: Graph-Consensus Interface
children.top_down_role: Peer-to-peer splitting over graph-coupled variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Consensus Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-based representation of peer-to-peer consensus on a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with an arbitrarily oriented incidence matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|\times |V|}\). For local variables \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stack \(x=(x_i)_{i\in V}\). Then the peer-to-peer consensus problem has the equivalent representation \[\min_x\sum_{i\in V}f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad (B\otimes I_d)x=0.\] Because \(G\) is connected, \(\ker(B\otimes I_d)=\{\mathbf{1}_{|V|}\otimes z:z\in\mathbb{R}^d\}\). Thus every constraint row couples only adjacent nodes, while feasibility is exactly global consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected graph, equality across every edge is equivalent to global consensus, so splitting can use only neighbor-to-neighbor communication.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
\(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper for each node \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B\otimes I_d)x=0\) holds if and only if \(x_i=x_j\) for all \(i,j\in V\).

notation.meaning: An oriented edge-node incidence matrix of the graph.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) maps \(X=\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) into itself.
There exists \(\tau<\infty\) such that \(0\le d_{k,j}\le\tau\) for every read.
Every block is activated infinitely often, and \(\lambda_k>0\) is chosen within a convergence-valid range when convergence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rule defines a bounded-delay partial-activation realization of the fixed-point iteration \(x=T(x)\).

notation.meaning: Set of block indices activated at event k.
Age of block j read at event k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate fixed-point interface with partial activation and boundedly delayed reads.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\), let \(T:X\to X\) have block components \(T_i:X\to\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\), and prescribe an initial history \(x^t=x^0\in X\) for \(t=-\tau,\ldots,0\). At event \(k\ge0\), activate a nonempty set \(S_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\), form the delayed read \(\widehat{x}^k=(x_j^{k-d_{k,j}})_{j=1}^p\), where \(0\le d_{k,j}\le\tau\), and choose \(\lambda_k>0\). Update \[x_i^{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_i^k+\lambda_k\bigl(T_i(\widehat{x}^k)-\widehat{x}_i^k\bigr),&i\in S_k,\\x_i^k,&i\notin S_k.\end{cases}\] A stopping test that combines multiple blocks must be evaluated at a declared consistent snapshot; otherwise the interface reports the latest block states together with their event counters and recorded delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each event updates selected blocks using possibly stale state, leaves inactive blocks unchanged, and records delays so any termination test combining blocks can be assessed from a declared consistent snapshot.

children.title: Solver Lifecycle Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Implementation policies connecting scaling, initialization, termination, and repeated solves.

children.title: Primal-Dual Scaling Interface
children.top_down_role: Coordinate and data scaling for balanced primal-dual behavior.

children.title: Operator Equilibration
children.top_down_role: Balancing interfaces applied to rows, columns, blocks, or operator components.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Equilibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal row-and-column equilibration of the linear coupling operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), positive diagonal matrices \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) and \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) constitute an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-operator equilibration when, for every nonzero row and column, \[\lVert e_i^{\mathsf T}DKE\rVert_2=\alpha\quad\text{and}\quad \lVert DKEe_j\rVert_2=\beta.\] An approximate equilibration with relative tolerance \(\eta\in[0,1)\) replaces each equality by membership in \([(1-\eta)\alpha,(1+\eta)\alpha]\) or \([(1-\eta)\beta,(1+\eta)\beta]\), respectively. Structurally zero rows and columns are excluded and must remain zero under diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal row and column scalings equilibrate an operator when all nonzero scaled rows and columns have prescribed, approximately equal norms.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite real matrix.
\(D\) and \(E\) are diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled coupling operator \(\widetilde K=DKE\) satisfies the stated row-and-column norm balance.

notation.meaning: Positive diagonal row and column scaling matrices.
Coordinate basis vector of the required dimension.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible definition of exact and approximate Euclidean row-column equilibration, but no source supports the prescribed common norms, tolerance convention, or treatment of structural zeros. The selected kind is also better characterized as a definition than a condition. An authoritative matrix-scaling or solver reference is required.

children.title: Problem Scaling
children.top_down_role: Coordinate, data, and objective rescaling across the represented model.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible primal, dual, constraint, and objective scaling of a linearly constrained convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\). Let \(E_x,E_z,D\) be invertible matrices and \(\gamma>0\), and set \(x=E_x\widetilde x\), \(z=E_z\widetilde z\). The equivalent scaled problem is \[\min_{\widetilde x,\widetilde z}\ \widetilde f(\widetilde x)+\widetilde g(\widetilde z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \widetilde A\widetilde x+\widetilde B\widetilde z=\widetilde c,\] where \(\widetilde f=\gamma f\circ E_x\), \(\widetilde g=\gamma g\circ E_z\), \(\widetilde A=DAE_x\), \(\widetilde B=DBE_z\), and \(\widetilde c=Dc\). If \(y\) and \(\widetilde y\) are unscaled and scaled Lagrange multipliers, then \(y=\gamma^{-1}D^{\mathsf T}\widetilde y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible variable and constraint transformations, with positive objective scaling, produce an equivalent problem and an explicit transformation of its dual multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(E_x,E_z,D\) are invertible and \(\gamma>0\).
\(f\) and \(g\) are extended-real-valued functions on compatible finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible points and objective ordering correspond bijectively, with \(y=\gamma^{-1}D^{\mathsf T}\widetilde y\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal transformation and stated multiplier relation are algebraically consistent with scaling the entire objective by \(\gamma\), but no citation verifies that this is the intended primal-dual scaling convention for the terminal container. A direct source is required before accepting the representation.

children.title: Scaling Reversal Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Recovery and reporting of solver outputs in the model's original coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Reversal Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of original primal-dual variables and residuals after an invertibly scaled solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given scaled outputs \((\widetilde x,\widetilde z,\widetilde y)\) for the scaling \(x=E_x\widetilde x\), \(z=E_z\widetilde z\), \(\widetilde A=DAE_x\), \(\widetilde B=DBE_z\), \(\widetilde c=Dc\), and objective factor \(\gamma>0\), recover \[x=E_x\widetilde x,\qquad z=E_z\widetilde z,\qquad y=\gamma^{-1}D^{\mathsf T}\widetilde y.\] Recompute the original-coordinate primal residual as \(r_p=Ax+Bz-c=D^{-1}\widetilde r_p\), rather than reporting \(\widetilde r_p\). Any dual residual, objective value, and certificate must likewise be transformed according to the declared scaling before comparison with original-coordinate tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface unscales primal and dual solutions, recomputes original-coordinate residuals and objectives, and applies tolerances only after reversal.
assumptions_latex: All scaling maps are recorded and invertible.
Scaled and original multipliers use the Lagrangian sign convention stated in the scaling representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported point and residuals are expressed in the original problem coordinates and units.

notation.meaning: Primal residual in scaled constraint coordinates.
Primal residual in original constraint coordinates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit primal and multiplier reversal formulas are consistent with the preceding scaling record, but the broader requirements for dual residuals, objectives, certificates, and tolerance comparison are unspecified and unsupported. A solver or scholarly source defining the complete reversal interface is required.

children.title: Solver Outcome Reporting System
children.top_down_role: Solver-facing presentation of residuals, gaps, tolerances, and status.

children.title: Termination Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Solver-facing categories for successful, unsuccessful, indeterminate, or interrupted termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Status Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually exclusive solver statuses determined by residual tests, certificates, and resource limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At termination, assign exactly one status using the following precedence. Report \(\mathrm{SOLVED}\) if the declared primal, dual, and gap tests all pass. Otherwise report \(\mathrm{PRIMAL\_INFEASIBLE}\) or \(\mathrm{DUAL\_INFEASIBLE}\) only if a corresponding certificate passes its verification test. If neither conclusion is certified and a numerical breakdown occurs, report \(\mathrm{NUMERICAL\_ERROR}\); if a declared iteration, time, or resource limit is reached, report \(\mathrm{LIMIT\_REACHED}\); otherwise report \(\mathrm{INDETERMINATE}\). The record must include the triggering predicate and final residual values, so a status is never inferred merely from lack of convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver reports solved or infeasible only after explicit tests pass; numerical failures, resource limits, and unresolved runs receive distinct nonconclusive statuses.
assumptions_latex: All tests and their tolerances are fixed before classification.
Certificate predicates are evaluated in original problem coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported status is unique and distinguishes certified conclusions from nonconclusive termination causes.

notation.meaning: All declared approximate optimality tests passed.
No certified conclusion or more specific termination cause applies.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a proposed classification algorithm rather than a mathematical condition. Its status vocabulary and precedence between numerical error, resource limits, and indeterminate termination are implementation-specific and have no cited normative source.

children.title: Certificate Reporting
children.top_down_role: Presentation of residual, gap, infeasibility, or unboundedness evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Reporting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-checkable reporting contract for approximate optimality or infeasibility witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate report is a tuple \(C=(t,w,s,m)\), where \(t\) is the claimed conclusion, \(w\) is a witness in original coordinates, \(s>0\) fixes its normalization, and \(m\) contains computed verification metrics. A verifier applies a declared predicate \(V_t(w/s;P,\varepsilon_t)\) to the original problem data \(P\). The report certifies \(t\) if and only if every component of \(V_t\) is satisfied at tolerance \(\varepsilon_t\). The report must include the witness, normalization, norms, inner products or objective quantities used by \(V_t\), and the applied absolute and relative tolerances; a status label alone is not a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate includes an original-coordinate witness, normalization, verification metrics, and tolerances sufficient for an independent checker to validate the claimed outcome.
assumptions_latex: The certificate type \(t\) has a fully specified verification predicate \(V_t\).
The reported witness has been reversed from all internal scalings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance of \(V_t(w/s;P,\varepsilon_t)\) is a reproducible certificate for the reported claim \(t\).

notation.meaning: Verification predicate for certificate type t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind fits the leaf, but the generic tuple and verifier predicate do not define a concrete optimality or infeasibility certificate. Because the predicate, normalization, and required metrics depend on the problem class, a direct standard or solver source is necessary.

children.title: Tolerance Reporting
children.top_down_role: Presentation of requested thresholds, achieved values, and scale conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Reporting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auditable residual-threshold record for an approximate primal-dual termination decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each termination metric \(r_j\) with scale quantity \(q_j\), report \(\lVert r_j\rVert\), \(q_j\), absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\), relative tolerance \(\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), and threshold \[\tau_j=\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{rel}}q_j.\] The associated test passes exactly when \(\lVert r_j\rVert\le\tau_j\). The report must identify the norm, coordinate system, iteration, and data used to form \(q_j\), and must separately list every required primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, stationarity, and gap test. A solved status is certified by this report only when every test declared mandatory by the solver has passed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Report every residual, scale term, norm, absolute and relative tolerance, and resulting threshold so the approximate termination decision can be independently reproduced.
assumptions_latex: Every required metric is evaluated at one consistent terminal iterate.
Residuals and scale quantities use the original problem coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The report permits direct verification of each inequality \(\lVert r_j\rVert\le\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{rel}}q_j\).

notation.meaning: A reported termination residual or gap metric.
Scale quantity used in the relative tolerance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold formula is a plausible reporting pattern, but the record does not specify the metric-dependent scale quantities or the mandatory tests for a particular primal-dual problem. Calling the report itself a certificate also requires a sourced definition of what conclusion it certifies.

children.title: Indeterminate Outcome Reporting
children.top_down_role: Reporting regimes where available evidence does not justify a definitive solver status.

knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Outcome Reporting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reporting boundary when no approximate solution or infeasibility conclusion has been certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an iteration terminates but neither the complete solved predicate nor any declared infeasibility-certificate predicate is satisfied. Then the interface must not report \(\mathrm{SOLVED}\), \(\mathrm{PRIMAL\_INFEASIBLE}\), or \(\mathrm{DUAL\_INFEASIBLE}\). It reports an indeterminate outcome together with the stopping cause, terminal iterate, residual and gap metrics, elapsed resources, and any failed certificate metrics. Reaching \(k=K_{\max}\), stagnating with \(\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\) small, or observing residual decrease without crossing tolerance is insufficient for a mathematical conclusion; each is only diagnostic evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If no solution or infeasibility test passes, termination is nonconclusive and must expose its cause, final metrics, resource use, and failed certificate checks.
assumptions_latex: The run has terminated under a declared operational stopping rule.
No complete conclusive-status predicate passes at the terminal state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The only mathematically sound outcome class is nonconclusive, with diagnostics rather than an optimality or infeasibility claim.

notation.meaning: Reported primal or composite solver iterate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind appropriately captures the prohibition on claiming a conclusive outcome when no required predicate passes. However, the required reporting fields and named statuses are normative, implementation-specific claims with no supporting source.

children.title: Sequential-Solve State Transfer Interface
children.top_down_role: Reuse across parameter paths, related models, and sequential solves.

children.title: Parameter Continuation
children.top_down_role: Sequential solves organized along regularization, penalty, or model-parameter paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Continuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential solution along a parameter path using neighboring terminal states as initial states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\theta)\) be a family of optimization problems and choose a schedule \(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_L\). Solve \(P(\theta_0)\) from a declared initial state \(s_0^0\). For \(\ell=1,L\), transform the preceding terminal state by a compatibility map \(M_{-1\to}\) and initialize \[s_^0=M_{-1\to}(s_{-1}^{\mathrm{term}}).\] Solve \(P(\theta_)\), optionally refine the schedule when convergence diagnostics exceed declared limits, and continue until \(	heta_L\). Each stage must re-evaluate feasibility and stopping tests for its own problem; acceptance at stage \(-1\) does not certify stage \(\). Output the terminal solution and a log of all schedules, transfers, and stage statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a parameterized sequence, initialize each stage from a compatibility-transformed prior state, and independently certify every stage under its own data and tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The parameter schedule and state compatibility maps are defined.
Each stage solver accepts the transferred state or a specified fallback initialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a state for \(P(\theta_L)\) without treating earlier-stage convergence as its certificate.

notation.meaning: Optimization problem indexed by continuation parameter theta.
Terminal algorithmic state at stage ell.
Compatibility map between consecutive stage states.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits parameter continuation, but the mathematical statement is corrupted: the stage index is missing from the loop, problem instances, states, and compatibility maps, and the range written as \(\ell=1,L\) is not a valid iteration range. Because no source is supplied to establish the intended interface and formulas, a sourced reconstruction is required.

children.title: Iterate Warm Starting
children.top_down_role: Reuse of primal, dual, or auxiliary iterates for a related solve.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Warm Starting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization of a new primal-dual solve from a compatible previous iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a new problem instance with state spaces \(X'\), \(Z'\), and \(Y'\), let a prior terminal state be \((x,z,y,u,\rho)\). Apply declared compatibility maps and initialize \[x'^0=M_xx,z'^0=M_zz,y'^0=M_yy.\] If a scaled dual variable is used, set \(u'^0=y'^0/\rho'\) for the new penalty \(\rho'>0\), rather than copying \(u\) when \(\rho'\neho\). Recompute cached products, factorizations, residuals, and stopping thresholds from the new problem data. If any map is undefined or a transferred value violates a required domain, replace that component by its declared cold-start value. Output the initialized state and transfer metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer compatible primal and dual iterates, rescale penalty-dependent dual state, rebuild data-dependent caches, and cold-start any incompatible component.
assumptions_latex: Compatibility maps \(M_x,M_z,M_y\) preserve dimensions and declared variable semantics.
The new penalty satisfies \(\rho'>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting state is internally consistent with the new instance and its scaled-dual convention.

notation.meaning: Scaled dual variable for penalty rho.
State-transfer maps for primal and dual components.
Penalty parameter of the new solve.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic kind fits warm-start initialization, and rescaling a scaled dual variable when the penalty changes is plausible. However, the displayed initialization concatenates symbols such as \(M_xx\) instead of explicitly applying maps, while domain compatibility, fallback behavior, and cache invalidation are unsupported implementation contracts. A direct source is required.

children.title: State Transfer Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Mapping retained solver state between related model instances.

knowledge_statements.title: State Transfer Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface contract for transferring ADMM state between parameterized problems with compatible block structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\theta)\) denote a family of problems \(\min_{x,z} f_\theta(x)+g_\theta(z)\) subject to \(A_\theta x+B_\theta z=c_\theta\). An ADMM state-transfer interface is a map \(\mathcal T_{\theta\to\theta'}\) sending \(s=(x,z,y,\rho,M,\mathcal C)\) to an admissible initialization \(s'=(x',z',y',\rho',M',\mathcal C')\) for \(P(\theta')\). It must validate block dimensions and domains, transport or discard incompatible cached data, and preserve the dual convention: if scaled duals are stored, then \(u'=y'/\rho'\). The interface returns the transferred state together with validity flags; invalid components are replaced by specified cold-start values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-transfer interface maps primal, dual, penalty, metric, and cached solver data to a compatible new problem while validating dimensions and dual scaling.
assumptions_latex: \(f_\theta\) and \(g_\theta\) are proper functions on specified finite-dimensional block spaces.
The source and destination problems expose their block dimensions and scaled-versus-unscaled dual convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_{\theta\to\theta'}(s)\) is either an admissible state for \(P(\theta')\) or a flagged partial transfer completed by declared cold-start defaults.

notation.meaning: factorizations, proximal caches, and other reusable computational data

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the interface leaf and is internally coherent, but the cited general ADMM section does not specifically support the proposed state-transfer contract, cache handling, validity flags, or cold-start defaults. A solver-lifecycle or warm-start interface source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Warm-Start Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model changes or incompatible states that negate the benefit of initialization reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of warm starting when successive problems or stored solver conventions are not uniformly compatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider sequential problems \(P(\theta_j)\) and a transfer rule producing initial state \(s_j^0\) from the terminal state of \(P(\theta_{j-1})\). No uniform warm-start improvement follows without a bound relating solution sets and transferred states: if \(P(t)=\min_x \tfrac12(x-t)^2\), the previous exact solution \(x^0=t_0\) has new-problem error \(|x^0-t_1|=|t_0-t_1|\), which is arbitrarily large. Likewise, retaining a scaled dual \(u\) while changing \(\rho\) replaces its represented multiplier by \(y'=\rho'u\). Thus unbounded parameter jumps, incompatible dimensions or domains, and unrescaled dual conventions lie outside any general warm-start guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warm starts offer no uniform benefit under unbounded problem changes or incompatible state conventions; even the initial error or represented multiplier can become arbitrarily large.
assumptions_latex: The transfer rule reuses at least one previous primal or scaled-dual component.
No uniform solution-set continuity or penalty-ratio bound is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no problem-independent bound forcing the transferred initial error to be smaller than a cold-start error.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar example establishes that transferred primal error can be arbitrarily large, and the dual-scaling calculation is correct. It does not establish comparison with a cold start because no cold-start rule or error is defined. A source and a precise comparator are required for the general failure-boundary conclusion.

children.top_down_role: Failures associated with unrestricted direct extensions beyond two blocks.

children.title: Naive Multi-Block ADMM Divergence
children.top_down_role: The divergence boundary for unrestricted direct Gauss-Seidel extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Naive Multi-Block ADMM Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct three-or-more-block Gauss–Seidel ADMM lacks the unconditional convergence guarantee of classical two-block ADMM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge 3\), consider \(\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\). The naive multi-block ADMM sequentially minimizes the augmented Lagrangian over \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), using newly updated preceding blocks, and then performs one multiplier update. Convexity and solvability alone do not ensure convergence: there exist finite-dimensional instances with closed proper convex quadratic \(f_i\), linear constraints, and a solution for which the resulting affine fixed-point iteration has an iteration matrix \(G\) satisfying \(\rho(G)>1\). For an initialization with a component in an unstable invariant subspace, the iterates therefore diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct Gauss–Seidel extension of ADMM to three or more convex blocks can have an iteration matrix with spectral radius above one and diverge.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 3\) and the block subproblems are updated cyclically without correction or additional proximal stabilization.
The problem is finite-dimensional, convex, and has at least one primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classical two-block ADMM convergence does not extend unconditionally to the naive multi-block iteration.

notation.meaning: linear part of the multi-block ADMM state iteration on a quadratic instance
spectral radius of the iteration matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local scope are correct, and the stated phenomenon is standard, but the existential claim about a convex quadratic instance with spectral radius greater than one requires a specific published counterexample and theorem, example, or page locator.

children.title: Block Organization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of stability on grouping and sweep organization.

children.title: Block Grouping Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability changes induced by merging, splitting, or repartitioning variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Grouping Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Changing which variables form ADMM blocks changes the induced resolvents and may change stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a fixed separable constrained problem have elementary variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\). A grouping \(\mathcal G=(G_1,\ldots,G_q)\) induces block variables \(X_j=(x_i)_{i\in G_j}\) and an ADMM update operator \(T_{\mathcal G}\). Distinct groupings generally produce different operators because minimization within a grouped block is joint, whereas splitting the same variables applies sequential augmented-Lagrangian minimizations. Consequently, neither fixed points of intermediate block maps nor their averagedness constants are grouping invariant. In particular, regrouping a multi-block formulation into two blocks may restore the classical two-block regime, while refining it into three or more naive Gauss–Seidel blocks removes that unconditional guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jointly grouping variables and updating them as separate Gauss–Seidel blocks produce different operators, so a stable two-block formulation can lose its guarantee when refined.
assumptions_latex: Each grouping preserves the same feasible set and objective after identifying grouped coordinates.
Every displayed block subproblem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence properties of ADMM are not invariant under refinement or coarsening of the block partition.

notation.meaning: ordered partition of elementary variables into update blocks
ADMM state-update operator induced by the grouping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the claims about averagedness constants, intermediate fixed points, and restoration or loss of convergence guarantees under regrouping require an ADMM-specific source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Block Ordering Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability changes induced by permutation or sweep organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Ordering Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Seidel multi-block ADMM operators depend on the order of noncommuting block updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered block list \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_m)\), write the exact block-update maps as \(U_i\) and the primal sweep as \(S_\pi=U_{\pi_m}\circ\cdots\circ U_{\pi_1}\). If two updates do not commute, \(U_i\circ U_j\ne U_j\circ U_i\), then exchanging their positions changes \(S_\pi\) and hence changes the complete ADMM iteration operator, including its linearization and spectral radius on quadratic problems. Therefore a convergence or contraction estimate proved for one cyclic ordering cannot be transferred to another ordering without an additional commutativity, symmetry, or order-uniform estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because Gauss–Seidel block updates generally do not commute, permuting blocks changes the ADMM operator and can change its contraction or stability behavior.
assumptions_latex: The method performs a sequential Gauss–Seidel sweep over at least three blocks.
At least one pair of exact block-update maps fails to commute.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist permutations \(\pi\ne\pi'\) for which \(S_\pi\ne S_{\pi'}\); order-specific stability bounds are not automatically permutation invariant.

notation.meaning: state map for the exact update of block \(i\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Noncommutativity of two isolated update maps shows that their two-map compositions differ, but it does not by itself ensure that complete sweeps differ after composition with all remaining maps; surrounding maps can erase the difference. An ADMM-specific source or stronger nondegeneracy assumptions are needed. The property content kind otherwise fits the leaf.

children.title: Grouping-Ordering Interaction
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes governed jointly by the selected partition and update sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Grouping-Ordering Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouping determines the update maps, while ordering determines their noncommutative composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an ordered partition \((G_1,\ldots,G_q)\), let \(U_{G_j}\) be joint minimization over the variables in \(G_j\). The sweep operator is \(S_{(G_1,\ldots,G_q)}=U_{G_q}\circ\cdots\circ U_{G_1}\). Grouping and ordering do not generally act independently: replacing adjacent groups \(G_i,G_{i+1}\) by \(G_i\cup G_{i+1}\) replaces \(U_{G_{i+1}}\circ U_{G_i}\) by a joint map \(U_{G_i\cup G_{i+1}}\), which need not equal either sequential ordering. Hence a favorable permutation for one partition need not remain favorable after regrouping, and stability must be assessed for the complete ordered partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging blocks changes the update maps themselves, not merely their order, so ordering conclusions generally cannot be carried unchanged across different groupings.
assumptions_latex: The augmented-Lagrangian block minimizers are well defined.
No separability or commutativity condition forces joint and sequential minimization to coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(U_{G_i\cup G_{i+1}}\ne U_{G_{i+1}}\circ U_{G_i}\) and \(U_{G_i\cup G_{i+1}}\ne U_{G_i}\circ U_{G_{i+1}}\).

notation.meaning: a group of elementary variable blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is appropriately placed, but absence of a separability or commutativity condition does not imply that the joint and sequential maps are unequal for every instance. The conclusion should be existential or qualified as a possibility, and an ADMM-specific source is required.

children.title: Insufficient Multi-Block Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Failure of multi-block decompositions lacking corrective or proximal geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Multi-Block Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A block-separable proximal term is insufficient when it does not dominate destabilizing cross-block coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cyclic multi-block ADMM, suppose block \(i\) receives the proximal term \(\tfrac12\|x_i-x_i^k\|_{P_i}^2\) with \(P_i\succeq0\). Merely having \(P_i\succeq0\) does not establish stabilization. A convergence argument requiring a positive energy metric \(H\) fails whenever the assembled metric is singular on a nonzero coupled direction \(d\), namely \(d^\top H d=0\) while \(\sum_i A_i d_i\ne0\), or whenever a coupling-dominance inequality such as \(H-C\succcurlyeq0\) is violated for the relevant cross-block operator \(C\). In that regime the proximal correction supplies no coercive control of the destabilizing mode, so naive multi-block divergence remains admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite proximal terms do not stabilize multi-block ADMM if the assembled metric leaves a coupled direction uncontrolled or fails the required coupling-dominance inequality.
assumptions_latex: The convergence analysis is based on a quadratic Lyapunov metric \(H\).
The block coupling is represented by a symmetric comparison operator \(C\) in that analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(H\) is noncoercive on a coupled direction or \(H-C\not\succcurlyeq0\), the stated metric argument supplies no convergence guarantee.

children.title: Parameterization Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instabilities caused by incompatible stepsizes, degenerate metrics, or uncontrolled adaptation.

children.title: Incompatible Primal-Dual Stepsizes
children.top_down_role: Loss of stability from mismatch between coupling and metric scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Primal-Dual Stepsizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar primal-dual steps must be compatible with the norm of the linear coupling operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-dual splitting of \(\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)\) with scalar steps \(\tau,\sigma>0\), the standard sufficient compatibility condition is \(\tau\sigma\|K\|^2<1\). Outside it, the usual positive metric and averagedness argument is unavailable. Instability is concrete for the unrelaxed bilinear iteration with \(f=0\), \(g^*=0\), and scalar \(K=1\): \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\sigma x^k\) and \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\tau y^{k+1}\). Its matrix has determinant \(1\) and trace \(2-\tau\sigma\); when \(\tau\sigma>4\), one eigenvalue has modulus greater than \(1\), so generic iterates diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual condition is primal step times dual step times squared coupling norm below one; sufficiently severe violation yields an explicitly unstable bilinear iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a bounded linear operator between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
The displayed counterexample uses simultaneous state \((x^k,y^k)\) and no extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compatibility inequality is essential to the standard guarantee, and \(\tau\sigma>4\) produces divergence in the displayed scalar instance.

children.title: Uncontrolled Penalty Variation
children.top_down_role: Adaptive penalties whose variation falls outside the intended convergence regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Penalty Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable ADMM penalties require bounded variation and consistent conversion between scaled and unscaled dual states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let ADMM use penalties \(\rho_k>0\) and store the scaled dual \(u^k=y^k/\rho_k\). If \(\rho_k\) is changed to \(\rho_{k+1}\) while \(u^k\) is retained, then the multiplier represented before the next update becomes \(\widetilde y^k=\rho_{k+1}u^k=(\rho_{k+1}/\rho_k)y^k\). Thus an unbounded penalty ratio creates an arbitrarily large artificial dual jump even with unchanged primal variables. Moreover, variable-metric convergence results imposing bounded penalties or summable relative changes do not cover sequences violating those conditions. Penalty adaptation outside such controls therefore has no inherited fixed-penalty convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the penalty without rescaling the stored dual can create an arbitrary multiplier jump; uncontrolled or nonsummable changes fall outside standard variable-metric guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The implementation stores the scaled dual \(u^k\).
Penalty changes may have unbounded ratios or nonsummable relative variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without dual rescaling and a variation condition, fixed-penalty or controlled-variable-metric convergence results do not apply.

A variable-penalty or variable-metric ADMM convergence source with a theorem or section locator is required.

children.title: Degenerate or Incompatible Preconditioning
children.top_down_role: Metrics that fail to control coupling or preserve accessible block geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a bounded linear operator between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
The primal-dual method uses proximal maps in inverse primal and dual metrics whenever those inverses exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(T\) or \(\Sigma\) is singular, the inverse-metric formulation requires an additional generalized-metric specification; if both are positive definite but \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\|\ge 1\), the displayed coupled metric is not positive definite.

notation.meaning: coupled block metric in the positive-definite case

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioners must define the inverse metrics required by the algorithm and sufficiently dominate primal-dual coupling.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two preconditioning failure modes for a primal-dual splitting with bounded coupling operator \(K\). First, if a self-adjoint primal or dual metric operator \(T\succeq0\) or \(\Sigma\succeq0\) is singular, then an algorithm written using the inverse metrics \(T^{-1}\) and \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is not defined on the whole space unless a generalized inverse or restricted-space formulation is specified. Second, when \(T\succ0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\), the standard coupling condition \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\|<1\) is equivalent to positive definiteness of \(M=\begin{pmatrix}T^{-1}&-K^*\\-K&\Sigma^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\). At equality the metric is singular, and above the boundary it is indefinite, so the standard positive-metric convergence argument is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular metric operators require an explicitly generalized formulation, while positive-definite preconditioners must satisfy the coupling-norm bound for the standard coupled metric to remain positive definite.

children.title: Extrapolation Instability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Oscillation or divergence associated with excessive extrapolation.

children.title: Aggressive Relaxation Failures
children.top_down_role: Oscillation or divergence associated with relaxation beyond a stable regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggressive Relaxation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Over-relaxing an averaged splitting operator beyond its admissible interval can cause oscillation or divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be firmly nonexpansive and consider the relaxed fixed-point step \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(Tz^k-z^k)\). The standard uniform relaxation interval is \(0<\lambda<2\). This boundary is sharp over firmly nonexpansive maps: for \(Tz=0\) on \(\mathbb R\), the iteration is \(z^{k+1}=(1-\lambda)z^k\). At \(\lambda=2\), every nonzero initialization alternates between \(z^0\) and \(-z^0\); for \(\lambda>2\), \(|z^k|=|1-\lambda|^k|z^0|\) diverges. Hence relaxation at or above two has no uniform convergence guarantee for this operator class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For relaxed firmly nonexpansive iterations, the interval below two is sharp: relaxation two oscillates and larger relaxation diverges even for the zero map.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space.
The relaxation parameter \(\lambda\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform convergence over this operator class fails for \(\lambda\ge2\).

children.title: Excessive Inertia Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability associated with overly strong momentum or extrapolated state reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Excessive Inertia Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncontrolled inertial extrapolation can destroy boundedness even when the underlying fixed-point map is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the inertial fixed-point iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k+\alpha(x^k-x^{k-1}))\) with constant \(\alpha\ge0\). Nonexpansiveness of \(T\) alone does not permit arbitrary inertia. For the nonexpansive identity map \(T=I\) on \(\mathbb R\), the increments satisfy \(d^{k+1}=\alpha d^k\), where \(d^k=x^k-x^{k-1}\). If \(\alpha>1\) and \(d^1\ne0\), then \(|d^k|=\alpha^{k-1}|d^1|\) and \((x^k)\) is unbounded. If \(\alpha=1\), then \(x^k=x^0+k d^1\), which is also unbounded unless \(d^1=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inertia at least one can make an inertial fixed-point sequence unbounded even when the base operator is the nonexpansive identity map.
assumptions_latex: The inertial parameter \(\alpha\) is constant.
The two initial points satisfy \(x^1\ne x^0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the displayed nonexpansive map, \(\alpha\ge1\) permits unbounded iterates; nonexpansiveness alone is insufficient for inertial stability.

children.title: Compound Extrapolation Instability
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes produced by interacting relaxation and inertial effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Compound Extrapolation Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar counterexample in which inertia and over-relaxation are stable separately at the indicated baselines but unstable in combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(T(x)=-x/2\), whose unique fixed point is \(0\). Consider \(y^k=x^k+\beta(x^k-x^{k-1})\) and \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda(T(y^k)-x^k)\). With \(\beta=0.3\) and \(\lambda=1.2\), the recurrence is \(x^{k+1}=-0.98x^k+0.18x^{k-1}\), with characteristic polynomial \(r^2+0.98r-0.18\). This polynomial has a root of modulus greater than one. By contrast, setting \(\beta=0\) while retaining \(\lambda=1.2\) gives \(x^{k+1}=-0.8x^k\), and setting \(\lambda=1\) while retaining \(\beta=0.3\) gives a recurrence whose characteristic roots both have modulus less than one. Thus the displayed instability arises from the combined parameter choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inertia and over-relaxation can be stable at their separate baseline settings yet make the combined scalar fixed-point recurrence unstable.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{-1},x^0\in\mathbb R\) are not chosen in the stable eigenspace of the combined recurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the combined parameters, \(\lvert x^k\rvert\to\infty\) for every initial pair outside the stable eigenspace.
review_flags: A supporting locator for compound inertial-relaxation instability is still required.
standard_field_rationale: the three scalar characteristic-polynomial calculations are directly checkable.

children.title: Execution Perturbation Failures
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns caused by ill-posed blocks, persistent computational errors, biased sampling, or excessive delay.

children.title: Ill-Posed Block Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Models for which an alternating block lacks a usable solution map.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Block Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure occurs when an augmented-Lagrangian block objective has no attainable minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linearly constrained model \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), the ADMM \(x\)-update requires a nonempty solution set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x)+\langle y^k,Ax+Bz^k-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz^k-c\rVert^2\). This requirement can fail. On \(\mathbb R\), take \(A=1\), \(B=0\), \(c=0\), \(g=0\), and \(f(x)=-\frac{\rho}{2}x^2-dx\) with \(d\ne y^k\). The quadratic terms cancel, leaving the nonconstant affine objective \((y^k-d)x\), which is unbounded below and has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: ADMM is not executable when a block augmented-Lagrangian minimization is unbounded below or otherwise fails to attain its infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ne y^k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x L_\rho(x,z^k,y^k)=\varnothing\), so the next ADMM iterate is undefined.

children.title: Persistent Inner-Solve Errors
children.top_down_role: Approximation errors that overwhelm outer splitting progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Inner-Solve Errors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-point model isolates failure caused by nonsummable inner-solve errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the exact splitting map \(T(x)=0\), so the exact iteration reaches its unique fixed point in one step. Model an inexact block solve by \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)+e^k\). If \(e^k=e\ne0\) for every \(k\), then \(x^{k+1}=e\) for every \(k\), and the fixed-point residual satisfies \(\lvert x^{k+1}-T(x^{k+1})\rvert=\lvert e\rvert\). Thus an error sequence that neither vanishes nor is controlled by a summability or relative-error condition can impose a permanent accuracy floor and invalidate convergence to the exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent inner error can keep every outer iterate a fixed positive distance from the exact splitting solution.
assumptions_latex: \(e\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\not\to0\) and the fixed-point residual remains \(\lvert e\rvert\).

children.title: Biased or Uncontrolled Stochastic Oracles
children.top_down_role: Sampling regimes incompatible with the stochastic convergence mechanism.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased or Uncontrolled Stochastic Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent oracle bias redirects stochastic approximation to a nonoptimal equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=\frac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), whose unique minimizer is \(x^\star=0\). Let the stochastic oracle return \(G_k(x)=x+b+\xi_k\), where \(b\ne0\), \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\), and the noise has uniformly bounded conditional second moment. For stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfying \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\) and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\), the recursion \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_kG_k(x^k)\) targets the zero of \(x+b\), not the zero of \(\nabla F(x)=x\). Under the usual stochastic-approximation stability conditions, its limiting equilibrium is \(-b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent oracle bias makes the stochastic iteration target a shifted equilibrium instead of the true optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\) and \(\sup_k\mathbb E[\xi_k^2\mid\mathcal F_k]<\infty\).
\(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\) and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle mean vanishes at \(-b\), and convergence to \(x^\star=0\) is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: history available before the iteration-k oracle call

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses biased stochastic splitting or its stability hypotheses.
standard_field_rationale: the conditional oracle mean equals x+b, so its equilibrium is shifted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shifted conditional mean is correct, but the asserted limiting equilibrium depends on unspecified stochastic-approximation stability conditions. A source and an explicit convergence hypothesis set are needed.

children.title: Asynchronous Consistency Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous regimes with excessive staleness or unsafe concurrent access.

children.title: Excessive Delay Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability or degraded progress caused by updates based on overly stale information.

knowledge_statements.title: Excessive Delay Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-step stale gradient can destabilize a stepsize that is stable synchronously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\frac12x^2\), synchronous gradient descent with stepsize \(\gamma=3/2\) obeys \(x^{k+1}=(1-\gamma)x^k=-\frac12x^k\) and converges to zero. If every update instead uses the one-step stale gradient, then \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\frac32x^{k-1}\). Its characteristic polynomial \(r^2-r+\frac32\) has complex-conjugate roots whose common modulus is \(\sqrt{3/2}>1\). Every nonzero real initial pair therefore produces an unbounded oscillatory sequence. Consequently, a stepsize admissible without delay need not remain admissible when the delay is introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even one stale iteration can destabilize a stepsize that contracts in the synchronous method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The delayed sequence is unbounded, whereas the synchronous sequence converges linearly to \(0\).

children.title: Concurrent Memory Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Corruption, inconsistency, or nondeterminism caused by unsafe shared-state access.

knowledge_statements.title: Concurrent Memory Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsynchronized full-state commits can repeatedly discard the progress of an otherwise convergent coordinate update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^2\), define \(T_1(x_1,x_2)=(x_2/2,x_2)\) and \(T_2(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,x_1/2)\). Their unique common fixed point is \((0,0)\), and repeated serial application of \(T_2T_1\) converges to it because the second coordinate is multiplied by \(1/4\) per composition. Now let two workers read the same current state in each round, compute \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), and commit entire vectors without synchronization. If the \(T_2\) commit always occurs first and the \(T_1\) commit always occurs last, the latter discards every change made by \(T_2\). The round-to-round shared state therefore follows \(x^{k+1}=T_1(x^k)\), which becomes constant at \((x_2^0/2,x_2^0)\) after one round and is nonzero whenever \(x_2^0\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflicting full-state commits can continually erase one worker's coordinate progress and prevent convergence even though the corresponding serial composition converges.
assumptions_latex: In each round both workers read the same pre-round state and overwrite the entire shared vector.
The \(T_2\) commit precedes the \(T_1\) commit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The concurrent execution satisfies \(x^k=(x_2^0/2,x_2^0)\) for every \(k\ge1\), so \(x^k\not\to(0,0)\).

children.title: Delay-Conflict Interaction
children.top_down_role: Asynchronous regimes where staleness and access conflicts jointly obscure failure attribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Conflict Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delay and overwrite conflicts jointly invalidate serial fixed-point semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1(x_1,x_2)=(0,x_2)\) and \(T_2(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,0)\), with common fixed point \((0,0)\). If workers may both evaluate an arbitrarily old snapshot and overwrite coordinates changed since that snapshot, then no execution-independent convergence conclusion follows from convergence of the serial composition \(T_2T_1\). In particular, delayed evaluations of the snapshot \((1,1)\) can continually generate \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\); conflicting full-state commits can alternately install these vectors. The resulting shared state cycles. Thus convergence analysis requires a consistency mechanism such as bounded staleness together with atomic or exclusive writes, or an equivalent bound on the aggregate perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stale reads combined with conflicting overwrites can sustain a cycle even though the serial operator composition reaches the solution immediately.
assumptions_latex: Read delays are unbounded or old computed updates may be committed indefinitely.
Writes may overwrite coordinates changed after the worker's read.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Serial convergence of \(T_2T_1\) does not imply convergence of the asynchronous shared-memory execution.

children.title: Nonconvex Global-Optimality Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between stationarity-oriented guarantees and global optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Global-Optimality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity is strictly weaker than global optimality for nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable nonconvex objective, a splitting method whose limit guarantee is only \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\) cannot thereby certify global optimality. Indeed, let \(F(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(F'(x)=4x(x^2-1)\), so \(\bar x=0\) is stationary, yet \(F(0)=1\), while \(F(1)=F(-1)=0\). Hence a residual expressing first-order stationarity can vanish at a point with a positive global objective gap. A global conclusion requires additional structure, such as convexity, an invexity-type property, or a separately verified global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonconvex problem, zero stationarity residual may occur at a point whose objective value is strictly above the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is given by \(F(x)=(x^2-1)^2\).

notation.meaning: limiting or classical subdifferential; here it equals the derivative

children.title: Nonunique Nonconvex Block Solutions
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity and instability caused by multiple local block solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Nonconvex Block Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonconvex block argmin may be set-valued, making the alternating update selector-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider alternating exact minimization of \(F(x,z)=(x^2-1)^2+(z-x)^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). At \(z^k=0\), the \(x\)-subproblem is \(\min_x x^4-x^2+1\), whose global minimizers are exactly \(x=\pm1/\sqrt2\). The subsequent \(z\)-subproblem has the unique solution \(z^{k+1}=x^{k+1}\). Therefore the block solution map at \(z^k=0\) has two separated values, and different admissible minimizer selectors immediately send the outer iteration to different states. Without uniqueness, a specified selection rule, or a set-valued convergence analysis, the phrase “the next block iterate” does not define a single algorithmic trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple global solutions of a nonconvex block problem make the alternating method set-valued and allow different valid trajectories.
assumptions_latex: Each block update selects an arbitrary global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(z^k=0\), the two valid next states include \((1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)\) and \((-1/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses nonunique nonconvex block solution maps.
standard_field_rationale: the two block argmin sets follow from elementary polynomial minimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two block minimizers and selector dependence are correctly calculated, but the record has no source locator supporting the nonunique nonconvex block-solution boundary.

children.title: Nonlinear Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of canonical linear-coupling structure and the need for specialized local methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Coupling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical ADMM splitting relies on affine coupling and does not transfer automatically to nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Classical two-block ADMM applies to the affine constraint \(Ax+Bz=c\), for which the augmented term is \(\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2\) and the multiplier enters through fixed adjoints \(A^*y\) and \(B^*y\). For a nonlinear constraint \(h(x,z)=0\), the KKT terms become \(D_xh(x,z)^*y\) and \(D_zh(x,z)^*y\), whose operators depend on the current blocks. For example, \(h(x,z)=xz-1\) gives multiplier terms \(zy\) and \(xy\). This system is not the same fixed linear-coupling monotone inclusion, so convergence theorems for canonical affine-coupled ADMM cannot be invoked without additional nonlinear regularity and a specialized local or linearized method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing affine coupling by a nonlinear constraint changes the KKT operator, so standard ADMM convergence theory no longer applies automatically.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable near the iterates.
The coupling is genuinely nonlinear, as in \(h(x,z)=xz-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical fixed-operator ADMM representation for \(Ax+Bz=c\) is unavailable without reformulation or linearization.

notation.meaning: partial derivatives of the coupling map

children.title: Weak versus Strong Convergence Boundary
children.top_down_role: The distinction between weak Hilbert-space convergence and norm convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak versus Strong Convergence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard basis of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space separates weak from norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), and let \(e_k\) denote its \(k\)-th standard basis vector. For every \(y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}\in H\), one has \(\langle e_k,y\rangle=y_k\to0\); hence \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\) weakly. However, \(\lVert e_k\rVert_2=1\) for every \(k\), so \(e_k\) does not converge to \(0\) in norm and has no strongly convergent subsequence. Therefore a Hilbert-space splitting theorem asserting only weak convergence of iterates cannot be read as a norm-convergence theorem without additional compactness, finite-dimensionality, uniform monotonicity, or another strengthening assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, weak convergence does not imply norm convergence; the standard basis is an explicit counterexample.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\) is equipped with its usual inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\) while \(\lVert e_k-0\rVert_2=1\) for all \(k\).

notation.meaning: the kth standard basis vector of \(\ell^2\)

children.title: Diagnostic Nonimplications
children.top_down_role: Cases where a commonly monitored quantity does not alone certify the desired optimization conclusion.

children.title: Small Residual without Objective Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Residual progress that may coexist with poor objective accuracy under scaling or degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual without Objective Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint scaling can make feasibility residuals arbitrarily small while leaving a fixed objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For parameters \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(M>0\), consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R} Mx\) subject to \(\varepsilon x=0\). The feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so the unique optimal point is \(x^\star=0\) with value \(0\). At the candidate \(\hat x=1\), the primal residual is \(r=\varepsilon\), whereas the objective gap is \(M\). Thus, for any residual tolerance \(\delta>0\) and any desired gap \(G>0\), choosing \(0<\varepsilon\le\delta\) and \(M\ge G\) yields \(\lvert r\rvert\le\delta\) but objective gap at least \(G\). No scale-independent objective-accuracy conclusion follows from a small primal residual alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling a constraint can make its residual arbitrarily small while the candidate retains an arbitrarily large objective gap.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\), \(M>0\), and residual means the unnormalized primal constraint residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no universal function \(\phi(t)\to0\) such that \(M\hat x-Mx^\star\le\phi(\lvert\varepsilon\hat x\rvert)\) for this family.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the problem
\[
\min_{x,z\in\mathbb{R}} f(x)+g(z) \quad \text{subject to} \quad x-z=0,
\]
where \(f(x)=g(z)=0\) for all \(x,z\in\mathbb{R}\). For the candidate sequence \(x^k=0\) and \(z^k=1\), the monitored objective values satisfy \(f(x^k)+g(z^k)=0\) for every \(k\), and hence their successive differences are zero. Nevertheless, the primal residual is \(r^k=x^k-z^k=-1\) for every \(k\). Thus objective stagnation, even at the optimal objective value of the constrained problem, does not imply primal feasibility and cannot by itself certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant objective sequence can remain persistently infeasible: zero objective change does not imply a vanishing constraint residual or certify a solution.

children.title: Iterate Stability without Optimality
children.top_down_role: Small iterate changes caused by damping, poor scaling, or inaccurate block solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Stability without Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A vanishing-step counterexample showing that small iterate changes need not indicate stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the unconstrained convex problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} h(x)=\tfrac12 x^2\), initialize \(x^0=1\) and apply the damped update
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_k h'(x^k)=(1-\alpha_k)x^k, \qquad \alpha_k=2^{-k-2}.
\]
Because \(0<\alpha_k<1\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k<\infty\), the iterates converge to \(\bar x=\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-\alpha_k)>0\), while \(\lvert x^{k+1}-x^k\rvert=\alpha_k\lvert x^k\rvert\to0\). Yet \(h'(\bar x)=\bar x\ne0\), so \(\bar x\) is not optimal. Therefore vanishing iterate differences alone do not certify stationarity or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable damping can make successive iterates arbitrarily close while they converge to a nonstationary, nonoptimal point.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert x^{k+1}-x^k\rvert\to0\) but \(h'(\bar x)\ne0\), so iterate stability does not imply optimality.

notation.meaning: damping or step-size parameter at iteration k
limit of the damped iterate sequence
